AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)

IAM is the AWS service that controls who can do what in an AWS account. It
is global, not tied to a single region, and it is the first thing most
engineers configure in a new account.

An IAM user represents a single person or application. Each user can have
long-term credentials: a password for the console, and access keys for the
CLI or SDKs. Best practice is to avoid creating long-lived access keys for
humans at all and to require multi-factor authentication for console
access.

An IAM role is different from a user: it has no long-term credentials of
its own. Instead, something -- a person, an application, or another AWS
service -- assumes the role and receives temporary credentials that expire.
Roles are the standard way to grant an EC2 instance or a Lambda function
permission to call other AWS services, instead of embedding access keys in
code.

Permissions in IAM are granted through policies, which are JSON documents
attached to a user, group, or role. A policy statement has an Effect
(Allow or Deny), an Action (which API calls it covers), and a Resource
(which specific things it applies to). By default, an IAM principal has no
permissions at all -- everything must be explicitly granted, and an
explicit Deny always overrides an Allow, no matter where else in the
account an Allow might otherwise apply.

The root user is the identity created when the AWS account itself is
created. It has unrestricted access and cannot be limited by any policy.
Because of that, AWS's own guidance is to lock the root user away: enable
MFA on it, avoid using it for daily work, and create IAM users or roles
with only the permissions actually needed for each job -- the principle of
least privilege.
